papers.title: “Why the face?”: Exploring Robot Error Detection Using Instrumented Observer Reactions
papers.authors: Maria Teresa Parreira, Ruidong Zhang, Sukruth Gowdru Lingaraju, Alexandra W.D. Bremers, Xuanyu Fang, Adolfo G. Ramirez-Aristizabal, Manaswi Saha, Michael Kuniavsky
papers.abstract: How do humans recognize and rectify social missteps? We achieve social competence by looking around at our peers, decoding subtle cues from others around us — a raised eyebrow, a laugh — to evaluate the environment and our actions. Robots, however, struggle to perceive and make use of these nuanced reactions. By employing a novel neck-mounted device that records facial expressions from the chin region, we explore the potential of previously untapped data to capture and interpret human responses to robot error. First, we develop NeckNet-18, a 3D facial reconstruction model to map the reactions captured through the chin camera onto facial points and head motion. We then use these facial responses to develop a robot error detection model which outperforms standard methodologies such as using OpenFace or video data, generalizing well especially for within-participant data. Through this work, we argue for expanding human-in-the-loop robot sensing, fostering more seamless integration of robots into diverse human environments, pushing the boundaries of social cue detection and opening new avenues for adaptable robotics.

papers.title: Visual World-Action Models for Embodied AI and Autonomous Driving: A Systematic Survey of Spatial Representations, Generative Dynamics, and Benchmarks
papers.authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels da Vitoria Lobo
papers.abstract: Here is the abstract as plain text, ready to paste into the submission form:Rapid progress in generative video modeling, 3D scene representation, and large-scale embodied datasets has catalyzed the emergence of World-Action Models (WAMs)—unified predictive frameworks that jointly model environment dynamics and agent actions over extended temporal horizons. Unlike reactive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that map current observations directly to motor commands, WAMs internalize physical causality, spatial geometry, and counterfactual outcomes to support closed-loop planning, simulation, and policy optimization. Recent surveys organize WAMs mainly by functional role and architectural coupling; fewer analyze them from a visual-computing perspective that contrasts how WAMs represent 2D, 3D, and 4D world states alongside physical accuracy and deployment latency. We establish a formal mathematical distinction between VLAs and WAMs, introduce a three-axis taxonomy spanning Latent Dynamics, Pixel/Video-Generative, and 3D/Occupancy-Centric paradigms, and compare 28 representative architectures across robotics and autonomous driving. We treat driving WAMs in depth, catalog 18 core benchmarks and simulators, and compile verified leaderboards of reported results on NAVSIM, nuScenes, Occ3D, LIBERO, and CALVIN. We further analyze the divergence between visual generation quality (e.g., FVD) and physical task success, formalize three physics-grounded diagnostics with an open-source reference implementation, and outline five open challenges with engineering remedies. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/awesome-visual-world-action-models.

papers.title: Vibe Coding AI Agents for an Educational Robot: Teacher Agency in Inclusive Language Education
papers.authors: 이성연
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) may offer responsive support for slow learners, particularly those who require more time, repetition, and scaffolded participation in language-related tasks. While research often uses the term “borderline intellectual functioning” for this group, in Korean educational and clinical contexts, the label of slow learners frequently overlaps with it. Here, slow learners refer operationally to learners whose slower learning pace requires sustained repetition, simplified sequencing, and closely guided instructional support. Drawing on Universal Design for Learning (UDL), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), and teacher agency, this exploratory qualitative study examined an eight-week extracurricular project in which four pre-service elementary teachers developed Gemini-powered prototypes and tested selected task-based agents on a Raspberry Pi 5-based robot for English language teaching on a Raspberry Pi 5-based robot. Data consisted primarily of two rounds of semi-structured interviews, supplemented by project materials. Findings show that teacher agency developed through implementation literacy, pedagogical editing of AI output, UDL-informed design rules, and negotiated engagement with vibe coding and robotic embodiment. Participants moved from consumer-level AI use toward more agentive design practices by revising prompts, hints, pacing, and interaction logic to meet pedagogical goals. Their TPACK development was evident in applying UDL principles to specific accessibility decisions. However, AI-assisted design was constrained by response delay, intention-output mismatch, and unstable behavior, particularly during robotic implementation. The findings suggest that pre-service teacher education should frame AI literacy as a design-and-judgment practice and provide mentoring that supports inclusive AI use.

papers.title: Mapping the AI Frontier: Semantic Topic Modeling and BERTopic Parameter Optimization— An Analysis of arXiv Preprints and a Practical Guide to UMAP/HDBSCAN Tuning
papers.authors: Pit Pichappan
papers.abstract: Semantic topic modeling has become an essential tool for mapping the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence research.While BERTopic has emerged as a leading framework due to its integration of transformer based embeddings and density-based clustering, practitioners frequently encounter degenerate clustering solutions such as single mega-clusters or artificial zero outlier states when relying on default library parameters.This study addresses this methodological gap by applying BERTopic to a curated dataset of 5,000 frontier arXiv AI preprints and conducting a systematic 90 configuration grid search to isolate the marginal and interactive effects of UMAP and HDBSCAN parameters.Our results reveal a critical, silent coupling between the two algorithms: UMAP's n_neighbors parameter manufactures the foundational density structure, silently redefining the meaning of HDBSCAN's min_cluster_size.Furthermore, we demonstrate that optimizing for single metrics like Density-Based Cluster Validation (DBCV) is fundamentally flawed, as it monotonically rewards overly tight, degenerate solutions.To resolve this, we propose a robust, multiobjective lexicographic filtering protocol and a practical, data-backed tuning guide.Applied to the arXiv corpus, this optimized framework successfully maps the AI frontier into distinct macro clusters (e.g., LLM/ Agent NLP vs. Embodied AI) while providing a reproducible methodology to prevent structural collapse in semantic topic modeling pipelines.

papers.title: Learning beyond rigid manipulation with hybrid soft-rigid robots
papers.authors: Mariano Ramírez Montero, Ebrahim Shahabi, Giovanni Franzese, Jens Kober, Barbara Mazzolai, Cosimo Della Santina
papers.abstract: Rigid-soft robot hybrids promise to unite the precision and repeatability of rigid manipulators with the compliance and adaptability of soft structures. Yet, full-fledged rigid-soft manipulators remain largely unexplored, in part because the intelligence required to exploit this combination is still missing. Here, we introduce a hybrid robotic system obtained by the series interconnection of a rigid arm and a soft manipulator, and systematically examine its ability to perform both established and previously inaccessible manipulation tasks. We show that a tailored imitation learning algorithm–generally applicable to this class of hybrid systems–leverages the complementary roles of rigid precision and soft embodiment to acquire manipulation skills and generalize them in a single shot across task variations. As a result, the system matches or exceeds the performance of rigid robots in classical tasks such as stacking, while enabling qualitatively new behaviors, including grasping objects through narrow openings.

papers.title: Embodied Intelligence: Definition, Clarification, Criteria, and Boundaries(具身智能:定义、澄清、判据与边界)
papers.authors: Yugui Yu
papers.abstract: Seventh paper of the human-referential fitting theory program. Between 2024 and 2026, "embodied intelligence" grew from a term in robotics and cognitive science into a word shared by policy documents, industry publicity, and academic surveys in many countries, without acquiring a stable definition; its parallel English names, embodied AI and physical AI, are in the same case. This paper extends the conceptual toolkit of the human-referential fitting theory to that term. (1) Definition: embodiment is a relational property of a system and an environment. A system S is embodied relative to an environment E if and only if its actions change the state of E through physical causation and its feedback comes from physical measurement (the physical closed loop), and its response latency lies below the characteristic time of the task-relevant physical process in E (timing prescribed by the environment). Embodied intelligence is the conjunction of two independent predicates, "embodied" and "intelligent"; it constitutes no new concept type but a restricted case of the capacity concept over physical environment classes. (2) Clarification: censuses of the English- and Chinese-language definitional corpus show that the existing disagreements have three sources: one limb of the conjunction written into the definition, the environment class left undeclared, and the level of the word left undistinguished. The three illicit slides each reappear in this discourse, joined by a fourth specific to it: conjunction confusion. (3) Criteria: the two conditions yield four executable tests (the closed-loop test, the body-swap test, the rollback test, and the pause test), and the timing margin gives a quantitative reading of "weak embodiment". (4) Distinctions and evidence: embodied intelligence implies neither the machine mind nor the world model; the claim that embodied intelligence is the road to AGI holds as a capacity claim but is not a conceptual inference as a route claim; and evidence from policy, think-tank, and corporate texts shows that systems which are embodied but lack the capacity, and systems which have the capacity but are not embodied, are both given the name. Seven falsifiability clauses, an admission protocol for new cases, and a survival clause close the paper.

papers.title: A part affordance dataset for semantic segmentation based on diffusion model
papers.authors: Xinyan Tan, Weimin Zhang, Fangxing Li, Zhengqing Zuo, Xiaohai He, Shicheng Fan, Chandan Sheikder
papers.abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation requires part-level perception and affordance understanding, yet constructing large-scale part-level datasets remains challenging due to costly and ambiguous annotations. To address this issue, we propose a training-free diffusion-based framework for automatic part-level affordance dataset construction. The framework progressively refines diffusion attention through a Part-Guided Semantic Field, a Local Subject Constraint Field, and a Bootstrap Self-Relational Enhancement Field, followed by SAM-based refinement to generate semantic segmentation masks. Evaluation on a manually annotated subset demonstrates strong agreement with human annotations, achieving 86.34% mIoU, 75.61% bIoU, 91.47% Dice, 91.46% precision, and 93.72% recall. Ablation experiments demonstrate the overall effectiveness of progressive attention refinement and SAM-based mask generation. An image-to-image extension further explores zero-shot part segmentation on real images, achieving 28.44% mIoU and revealing challenges in cross-domain generalization. These results demonstrate the feasibility of diffusion-based part-level pseudo-annotation and its potential to reduce manual annotation requirements.

papers.title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control
papers.authors: Lisiyu Pan, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Tang
papers.abstract: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/iMFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/iMFPO.

papers.title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Cross-Embodiment Robot Control
papers.authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Juntong Zhang, Li Zhang
papers.abstract: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.

papers.title: WorldPhy: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Physical Plausibility of World Models in Robotics
papers.authors: Ziyuan Chu, Mingzhi Zheng, Kaiyue Zhang, Jinan Zhang, Linchao Zhu
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.

papers.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Xu Yang, Kailai Sun, Qianchuan Zhao
papers.abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-ρ$, where $ρ$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.

papers.title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
papers.authors: Ajmain Istiak Apon, Md Mehedi Hasan, Sejuti Rahman
papers.abstract: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.

papers.title: WISER-RL: A Wake-Sleep Learning Mechanism for Robot Reinforcement Learning from One Demonstration
papers.authors: Kwunhang Wong, Yang Bai, Qingyang Bao, Liudi Yang, Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang, Lin Li, et al.
papers.abstract: A robot learning from one human demonstration may rarely succeed on its own, leaving reinforcement learning (RL) with little reward feedback. We introduce WISER-RL ({W}ake--sleep policy improvement loop, {I}mitation, and {S}elective {E}xperience {R}eplay), a composite reinforcement learning framework that turns assisted practice into autonomous control. During wake, GPTDAgger monitors disagreement among actions sampled by a diffusion policy. When disagreement crosses a threshold, a frozen GPT controller uses retrieved experience to continue the episode. During sleep, Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) compares visually matched successful trajectories and downweights conflicting action windows with more steps remaining to success. The policy imitates the reweighted successes and learns from both successes and failures through offline advantage-guided RL before collecting the next round. After final online PPO refinement, the autonomous policy succeeded in 100% evaluations on each of six LIBERO tasks and 100% trials on each of two real-robot tasks.

papers.title: WAtcher: Watching Ahead for Safe Robotic Manipulation with Efficient World-Action Models
papers.authors: Ziyu Shan, Xiao Ma, Kangrui Yu, Changjie Wang, Gaoyuan Wu, Zaijia Yang, Chuanrui Zhang, Qirui Li, et al.
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ~25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for $π_{0.5}$. papers.title: Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for Self-Supervised Video Representation Learning
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Siran Dai, Qingming Huang
papers.abstract: Self-supervised video representation learning has achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale unlabeled video data. Recent methods commonly extend Masked Image Modeling (MIM) to Masked Video Modeling (MVM), where video representations are learned by capturing semantic information from temporal contexts during masked content recovery. Unlike static images, videos exhibit inherent temporal variation, as visual objects continuously change their positions, appearances, and motion states across frames. Therefore, MVM needs to preserve semantic consistency while capturing temporal changes of corresponding regions, which raises two central challenges: 1) how to establish reliable temporal correspondence across frames, and 2) how to formulate an appropriate representation learning objective for modeling both semantic consistency and temporal variation. To address these challenges, we propose Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for video Representation learning (VT-CoRe) framework. For challenge 1), VT-CoRe introduces a sandwich sampling strategy to construct two-sided temporal references and a Patch Registration Module (PRM) to establish reliable patch-level correspondence. For challenge 2), VT-CoRe imposes latent-space semantic alignment on registered representations through a self-distillation architecture and further proposes temporal variation modeling to constrain representation trajectories over time. Experiments on 8 downstream tasks across 16 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of VT-CoRe across pixel-level, frame-level, video-level, and vision-based robotic learning scenarios. Complementary representation analysis shows that VT-CoRe learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware temporal correspondence learning.

papers.title: Trustworthy agentic AI systems: navigating the risks and governance of autonomous AI
papers.authors: Gregoris N. Mentzas
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. Unlike traditional GenAI, AgAI systems are capable of perception, planning, and independent action. This shift introduces a unique class of sociotechnical risks, including goal misalignment, cascading operational errors, and security vulnerabilities. This paper reviews the AgAI landscape, examines its architectural components (planning, memory, action, and multi-agent collaboration) and its transformative potential across key sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, robotics, and software development. By analyzing existing corporate and regulatory governance frameworks, the paper identifies gaps in accountability, liability, and real-time intervention. We argue that establishing trustworthy AgAI requires a shift from regulating content to constraining autonomous consequences, and propose seven research and governance challenges focusing on dynamic alignment, responsibility attribution, verifiable specifications, and standardized benchmarks, to ensure AgAI systems remain aligned with human values.

papers.title: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform
papers.authors: Zilin Huang, Zhengyang Wan, Zihao Sheng, Boyue Wang, Ruolin Yang, Yuhao Luo, Sikai Chen
papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models are increasingly deployed by selection: a practitioner picks a public checkpoint by benchmark rank and fine-tunes it on local data. The platform is fixed before the model is chosen, with little or no local data. We ask what such a checkpoint loses on a fixed platform and which part of the loss local data can buy back. We split the gap by what can repair it. A sensing gap, information the sensors do not capture, cannot be closed with their data; a latency gap, output arriving after the control loop needs it, belongs to the loop, not the weights; only a distribution gap is fine-tuning's to repair. TRIAGE turns this into feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation in five stages: gates on the sensor contract and on end-to-end latency that no score can override, probes on ten minutes of local logs, a ranking by target-relevant score among the candidates that pass, and fine-tuning that is monitored and checked in closed loop before release. On driving benchmarks, a deadline below a leading closed-loop model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes, and losing field of view moves plans 2.2 to 5.7 times more than losing resolution at equal pixels. Local frames close 75% of a stability gap but raise perturbation sensitivity at small budgets, and picking by score violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the factory camera failed the sensing gate and an added camera repaired it. The latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip. The selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips, and the closed-loop check withheld a fine-tuned model that had improved offline. TRIAGE lets organizations that cannot train foundation models from scratch find out whether a public checkpoint can run on the robot or vehicle they own, and what to fix if not.

papers.title: Towards 360$^\circ$ Embodied UAV Tracking Without Turning
papers.authors: Bingyu Li, Wu Du, Zhiyuan Zhao, Junyu Gao, Xuelong Li
papers.abstract: Conventional embodied UAV tracking couples target observability with heading control because targets may leave the field of view of forward-facing cameras. We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $π_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $π_{0.5}$. Our benchmark further reveals a substantial gap between offline imitation accuracy and closed-loop tracking reliability, establishing a challenging testbed for future research https://libingyu01.github.io/360UAV-ETrack_360UAV-TVLA/

papers.title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
papers.authors: Yuxiang Lai, Jike Zhong, Yu-Jhe Li, Lan Wang, Chengzhi Liu, Youbao Tang, Ming Li, Xi Xiao, et al.
papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.

papers.title: The prosocial robot navigation charter: a framework based on normative cards
papers.authors: Anthony G. Francis Jr.
papers.abstract: Recently, the social robotics community established a set of principles for social robot navigation, including safety, comfort, legibility, politeness, social norms, agent understanding, proactivity, and contextual awareness. These principles were developed to guide the design of algorithms that achieve social behavior implicitly, but recent advances enable guiding behavior explicitly with language instructions supplied to large language models. Furthermore, robotics foundation models enable zero-shot execution of open-set tasks while remaining safe for users, using techniques like visual-language understanding, grounded action models, and constitutional safety systems. These new features suggest an opportunity to use the social robot navigation principles as a constitution for social behavior for a language-based agent. Furthermore, these new capabilities suggest expanding the social navigation principles to support more sophisticated behaviors. Since language-based agents are capable of understanding their relationship to their users, nearby pedestrians, and the community, we argue that the next generation of socially navigating robots should be prosocial: that is, actively trying to improve the social navigation environment they operate in. This requires not merely being good pedestrians in the navigation environment, but good participants in the social environment—taking on tasks such as clearing obstructions, alerting others to hazards, and giving directions to passersby, as long as these tasks are within the robot’s capabilities and do not interfere with the robot’s goals. This paper reviews the social navigation principles, argues for a definition of prosocial robot navigation, and explores how literate artificial intelligence can use the research literature itself to guide agents. To ensure the resulting guidance is aligned with human expectations, the paper proposes a Normative Card Architecture which specifies how robots ought to behave in terms of schema-verifiable, machine-auditable, human-approved, automatically-assembled machine-readable charters for robotics agents that use language-model planning. The paper then describes a Prosocial Navigation Charter which implements the prosocial navigation principles in the Normative Card Architecture framework, and presents a proof-of-concept demonstration of the framework’s support for auditability.

papers.title: Targeted Adaptation of World-Action Models via Interaction and Motion Heads
papers.authors: Yuze Zhu, Jacky Li, Yusen Luo, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chancharik Mitra, Trevor Darrell, Roei Herzig
papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm of robot manipulation policies that jointly generate future video and actions. Successful manipulation requires both identifying where to interact and modeling how the robot and objects move. Yet standard adaptation methods, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, do not explicitly select parameters aligned with these manipulation-specific capabilities. Motivated by this challenge, we discover two functionally specialized families of attention heads: Next-Interaction Heads, which localize upcoming grasp-and-release targets, and Motion Heads, which track movement across frames. Furthermore, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that jointly adapts Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. On RoboTwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning, HeadLight achieves 62.28% success, compared with 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters. Inference-time ablations further validate the functional importance of these heads: ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads lowers it to 40.61%, both substantially more than ablating equally many random heads. Finally, we show that our approach is effective across multiple WAM architectures and real-robot manipulation settings.

papers.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
papers.authors: Chen Li, Aaron M. Hoover, Paul Birkmeyer, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Ronald S. Fearing, Daniel I. Goldman
papers.abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

papers.title: Starlight: Predicting Design Ranking Reversals in an Autonomous Cars from Measured Steering Gains
papers.authors: Aarav Jalan, Darsh Zaveri
papers.abstract: Engineers often choose designs through trial and error, but small calibration changes can reverse their performance rankings. Limited tests may also make uncertain choices appear decisive. Starlight investigates how recognizing these reversals can lead to more reliable decisions. We compared two bundles, A and D, each containing seven robot-design features, across 752,000 simulated missions. Our decision procedure used paired failure-rate differences and simultaneous uncertainty bounds, balancing the costs of further testing, incorrect selections and withholding judgment. It could select a winner, accept either design, reject both as inadequate or request more evidence. We compared it with seven baselines and three ablations. Paired physical docking trials tested Clock, which used preset turns, and Compass, which corrected heading through feedback, under controlled steering mismatch. Linkage-change trials and blind ratings assessed hardware effects, while colour sorting tested generalizability. A 5% steering-gain increase reversed simulated rankings: A led D by 1.050 percentage points at gain 1.200, while D led A by 2.925 at 1.260. The method withheld selection in 29 of 66 conditions and reduced overall decision cost by up to 33% against seven baselines. Clock’s mean heading shifted 6.42° under mismatch, compared with 0.48° for Compass. The ten-unit audit matched eight held-out references but made one unsupported winner call. In three-colour sorting, the framework favoured calibrated detection (S2) over fixed-threshold detection (S1), while accepting detection with rechecking (S3) as an alternative. To sum it up, Starlight shows how accounting for uncertainty improves calibration-sensitive robot-design decisions.

papers.title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Benjamin Fuhrer, Chen Tessler, Gal Dalal
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.

papers.title: SkySearcher: High-Altitude Onboard VLM Reasoning for Aerial Semantic Search
papers.authors: Giacomo Vianello, David Morilla-Cabello, Juan Dendarieta Serrano, Ruggero Carli, Eduardo Montijano
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.

papers.title: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery
papers.authors: Wenfang Sun, Jianghao Deng, Wenzhe Yin, Yingjun Du, Cees G. M. Snoek
papers.abstract: Robot agents discover reusable skills by revising programs from execution feedback and retaining experience for later tasks. This process can fail when an agent treats an unsuccessful program as evidence that the task is physically impossible, ending exploration with revision budget remaining. We study this failure in Qwen3.8-27B and examine two decisions that shape skill discovery: I) how execution failures are diagnosed, and II) which lessons enter the shared skill library. Failure diagnosis requires the agent to reconstruct physical action effects from multimodal traces, while independent reproduction of a proposed repair does not require adequate task performance from its source program. We introduce Skeptic, a training-free protocol that uses measured action outcomes to guide repair and measured task success to govern skill admission. A grounded event log reports action effects and object end states from depth images and proprioception, separating sensor observations from inferred diagnoses. Verified promotion adds a development-success requirement on the source program to the existing independent reproduction check. Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign. On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points, with frozen model weights and the same program-revision budget.

papers.title: Shared control/autonomy in human-robot interaction: Current trends and the role of generative AI
papers.authors: Michael Hagenow, Mario Selvaggio, Xuehui Yu, Yanwei Wang, Yiannis Demiris, Andreea Bobu, Yilun Du, Harold Soh
papers.abstract: In shared control and shared autonomy (SC/SA) systems, humans collaborate with robot agents to achieve common goals. Such systems enable collaborations beyond what either agent could do alone, benefiting from the relative strengths of humans (e.g., reasoning, planning) and robots (e.g., precision, repeatability). Research in this area dates back over 40 years, with numerous applications, such as in manufacturing, robot-assisted surgery, and assistive technologies. Shared control approaches have even seen some large-scale commercialization efforts in areas like semi-autonomous driving and automotive assembly. Without SC/SA, we may not have seen robots deployed in settings where manual teleoperation alone is too difficult, such as delicate laparoscopic surgical procedures or the remote operation of space manipulators. Recently, SC/SA approaches have gained significant traction, with hundreds of new methods published in scientific papers each year. In this paper, we examine recent approaches and trends in these methods, investigating several crucial aspects that are underexplored in previous surveys. We reviewed 195 papers across a 5-year time window (2020 to 2024) in three high-impact robotics venues (IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, and Science Robotics). First, we provide descriptive statistics and trends related to human input methods, technical approaches, and applications. Second, we provide a perspective on the growing role of generative artificial intelligence approaches in SC/SA. Based on these insights, we offer updated recommendations for future approaches.

papers.title: ScanAR: Parallel Row-Scan Decoding for Efficient Image Generation in Unified Autoregressive Models
papers.authors: Jingen Qu, Xi Chen, Yingbo Tang, Xinghang Li, Tao Kong
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal autoregressive (AR) models represent text and images in one token sequence and generate all modalities with a shared next-token prediction head. Their image generation, however, decodes an $H\times W$ visual grid token by token in raster order, which takes $HW$ sequential steps and dominates inference time. Existing acceleration methods for visual AR generation either change the tokenizer, the prediction head, or the model interface, or keep the model but cannot reach high parallelism without losing quality, so they do not carry over to unified AR models. We propose ScanAR, a row-scan parallel decoding method that only redefines the predecessors of visual tokens. The first visual row is generated from left to right as usual, and each later row is generated in a single parallel step, with every token predicted from the vertically aligned token of the previous row. Nonvisual tokens keep the standard autoregressive rule. ScanAR reduces the visual decoding depth from $HW$ to $H+W$ without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head and without adding parameters, and it supports both training from scratch and lightweight post-training. On Emu3.5-Image-34B, ScanAR post-training reaches a GenEval score of 82.36, the best among post-training acceleration methods trained on the same data, and generates $512\times512$ images $13.8\times$ faster than raster decoding under the same inference setting. On ImageNet, ScanAR trained from scratch has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster LlamaGen. On the 34B Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 model, ScanAR preserves the overall quality of embodied scene generation, interleaved image-text generation, and video generation.

papers.title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
papers.authors: Xiang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Ya-Li Li, Tao Li, Rui Zhang, Junjie Lai, Weihua Zhang, Shengjin Wang
papers.abstract: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

papers.title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Zeyang Guan, Qihao Zhao, Rui Gong, Zhang Haitian, Yalun Dai, Yangyu Huang, Lingao Xiao, Haozhe Du, et al.
papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. https://zeyangguan.github.io/SEEK-Agentic-Robot-Manipulation/

papers.title: Robot-assisted stereotactic catheter drainage vs. standard medical treatment for 20–30 mL basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage: a propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study
papers.authors: ChengYi Jin, Zhijian Fu, Ming Lei, Chunyi Xia, Zhipeng Tang, Dexin Ren, Mo Liu, Di Sun
papers.abstract: Objective: To investigate whether robot-assisted stereotactic catheter drainage was associated with better functional recovery than standard medical treatment in selected patients with basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage (BGICH) and a hematoma volume of 20–30 mL. Methods This single-center, retrospective, propensity score-matched cohort study included patients with BGICH treated at Shenyang First People's Hospital of Liaoning Province between June 2022 and December 2025. Patients were classified into the operation or non-operation group according to the treatment actually received in routine clinical practice. Propensity score matching was performed to reduce baseline imbalance and treatment-selection bias. Short-term neurological recovery, in-hospital outcomes, and 90-day functional outcomes were compared between the two groups in the matched cohort. Results Among 287 screened patients, 165 met the eligibility criteria, including 103 patients in the operation group and 62 in the non-operation group. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 53 matched pairs were included in the primary analysis, with adequate balance in baseline characteristics. Compared with the non-operation group, the operation group had a shorter length of hospital stay, higher upper- and lower-limb muscle strength at discharge, and higher rates of limb muscle strength improvement. At 90 days after symptom onset, the operation group had lower modified Rankin Scale scores and higher Glasgow Outcome Scale and Karnofsky Performance Scale scores than the non-operation group. No significant differences were observed in common in-hospital complications or in the recovery of dysphagia or dysarthria. Conclusion In selected patients with 20–30 mL BGICH, robot-assisted stereotactic catheter drainage was associated with better early limb motor recovery, shorter hospitalization, and more favorable 90-day functional outcomes. Because treatment was not randomized and post-discharge rehabilitation exposure was incompletely quantified, these findings are exploratory. Further assessment using prospective data is warranted.

papers.title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
papers.authors: Ben Ma, Jixuan Cai
papers.abstract: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

papers.title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
papers.authors: Chenzhi Liu, Jiehong Lin, Wei Huang, Xuzhao Huang, Haoyuan Li, Yang Zhang, Junchao Huang, Chenyeyang Cai, et al.
papers.abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

papers.title: Riding the Wave: Sim-to-Real Humanoid Control on Elastic Terrain
papers.authors: Yinglei Zhu, Qin Li, Honghao Pan, Bozhao Wang, Binghui Xu, Jie Lu, Wentao Song, Xiyu Wang, et al.
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots on deformable elastic terrains face a surface whose position and motion are coupled in space and time: deflection and rebound persist between contacts, and load at one foothold alters the support at others, so training must capture how each contact changes the support that follows. We present RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on such terrains. RIPPLE integrates ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh that models spatially coupled deflection, energy storage, and rebound, together with deformable contact into MJLab for GPU-parallel policy learning. Staged training then transfers rigid-ground skills to balance and jumping on these terrains using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Deployed zero-shot, the policies enable a MagicBot Z1 humanoid to balance, jump consecutively, and enter a trampoline from a rigid platform. In simulation, ElasticMembrane training holds standing success of at least 98.7% (mean over three seeds) on ElasticMembrane, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate under 0.3 m/s perturbations, whereas rigid-ground or contact-compliance training transfers poorly to the first two. A fixed policy tolerates stiffness from 0.35 to 2.8 times the training value, beds up to 7 m wide, and seven further simulated support scenarios, so transfer needs no calibration to the trampoline's stiffness. papers.title: Reinforcement learning control of a Brayton cycle heat pump: a model-to-implementation study via Software-in-the-Loop
papers.authors: Phong Tran, Fatma Cansu Yücel, Panagiotis Stathopoulos
papers.abstract: Decarbonising industrial heating requires high-temperature heat pumps, and Brayton cycle heat pumps are a promising option. Ensuring safe and efficient control of these systems, however, remains challenging. This study introduces an experimentally validated dynamic model of a Brayton heat pump to train control strategies involving Reinforcement Learning (RL) and traditional PI controllers, and a combination of both. The RL agents were trained with domain randomisation, and the resulting controllers were evaluated via offline simulations and a Software-in-the-Loop (SitL) setup. Offline simulations demonstrated that RL accurately tracked target temperatures, maintained safety margins, and discovered an efficiency-improving pressure manipulation strategy. The subsequent SitL study assessed integration feasibility in the target execution environment, where all controllers operated stably and adhered to the safety constraints under the settings intended for physical operation. In this configuration, the RL controllers did not outperform the PI baseline in efficiency. The presented workflow transfers a learned controller from the plant model to the environment used to operate the demonstrator, and identifies deployment effects before commissioning.

papers.title: Rehearse in 3D, Render in 2D: Physically Consistent and Editable Robot World Models
papers.authors: Guangyu Liu, Hanzhang Wang, Huijia Zhang, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang, et al.
papers.abstract: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.

papers.title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
papers.authors: Shengming Liu, Yunyi Gao, Xinyi Wang, Jianyong Sun, Shuai Wang, Yi Deng, Li Chenye, Mingcai Zhou, et al.
papers.abstract: Code-as-Policy agents generate, execute, and revise robot programs, but often lack explicit mechanisms to govern what persists across executions: which actions are retained within a trial and which code modifications carry over to subsequent runs. This leaves two critical aspects of agent behavior insufficiently controlled: step-level execution and cross-run adaptation. We present RegHarness, a two-level harness that governs both forms of persistence for the RATs agent team, without relying on a vision-language-action (VLA) policy or demonstrations. Within each trial, run-time governance evaluates each proposed step from a reset scene, replaying the committed steps, while a fixed-rule controller commits the step only when both RATs' verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve it. Between runs, a coding agent uses logged failures to develop and test revisions to skills, primitives, and rules, which remain disabled by default until explicitly enabled by the authors. Using a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials. A $2\times2$ ablation study of RegHarness's two levels shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46. These findings suggest that, for Code-as-Policy agents operating with low-cost models, task success depends not only on how generated programs are executed, but also on the quality of the reusable skills they invoke and how those skills evolve across runs.

papers.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
papers.authors: Yang Guan, Shengbo Eben Li
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.

papers.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.authors: Insup Lee, Hojin Jeon, Sunguk Shin, Seoungbin Bae, Taekwan Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Dongsu Han
papers.abstract: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.

papers.title: Precision apiculture in practice: performance of robotic hives vs. traditional hives in almond pollination
papers.authors: Rya Seltzer, Inna Goldenberg, Judith Nathanson, Paz Kahanov, David Sanderovich, Shlomki Frankin, Hallel Schreier, Arnon Dag
papers.abstract: Pollination by managed honey bee (Apis mellifera) colonies underpins modern agriculture but faces challenges, including declining colony health and increasing climate variability. Precision apiculture, integrating robotics and data-driven monitoring, offers a promising path toward more efficient beekeeping and pollination events, but field-scale validation remains limited. We deployed 448 colonies representing the two hive types across eight plots in a 64-ha commercial almond orchard. Within this large-scale deployment, we monitored entrance activity in 32 focal colonies, flower visitation on32 “Nonpareil” and 32 “ Butte ” trees, and fruit set on 32 “ Nonpareil ” trees. A significant interaction between hive type and time of day was detected (LMM: F 9,1657 · 60 = 2.26, p = 0.016). BH colonies exhibited a more pronounced midday rise in entrance activity. Flower visitation and fruit set were similar between hive types, but foraging varied strongly among cultivars: “ Nonpareil” averaged 16.2 bees per tree per minute, whereas the late-blooming pollinizer “Butte” reached 47.2. The observed difference may reflect cultivar-specific attractiveness, bloom progression, or changes in the spatial distribution of floral resources. Overall, both hive systems delivered strong pollination. However, the elevated and temporally structured activity in BH colonies suggests potential advantages under cooler or otherwise suboptimal conditions, supporting the value of precision-apiculture technologies for maintaining strong, balanced colonies after pollination.

papers.title: Practice Makes Fluent: Learning to Use Earlier Predictions in Looped Models
papers.authors: Minseok seo, Hee-Seon Kim, Changick Kim
papers.abstract: People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation. We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice. This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes. We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost. FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in new Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth. On a real robot, success rises from 62.3\% to 74.6\% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69\,s to 31\,s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.

papers.title: Physical Artificial Intelligence-Driven Robotic Platform for Autonomous Intravascular Injection and Pharmacokinetic Applications
papers.authors: Kyeong‐Ryoon Lee, Yoon‐Jee Chae, Jaeyoung Lee, Hyeon-Cheol Jeong, Ryeo-Won Kim, Hui‐Jeong Gwon, Ki‐Suk Kim, Ki‐Hwan Nam
papers.abstract: Tail vein intravenous injection in mice is a fundamental procedure used in preclinical, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacological studies; however, it remains highly operator-dependent and susceptible to variability and extravasation. To address these limitations, we developed a physical artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated intravascular injection system (AIIS) that integrated deep-learning-based vision, robotic actuation, optimized optical illumination, and real-time pressure feedback within a closed-loop control framework. The AIIS employed a DeepLabv3 + convolutional neural network for real-time tail vein segmentation under wavelength-optimized green light-emitting diode illumination (525–550 nm), enabling robust vein recognition across mouse strains with differing tail pigmentation. Vision-based alignment, robotic micro adjustments, and pressure-based confirmation of venous entry facilitated autonomous and precise needle insertion and achieved high injection success rates of 90%–96% with submillimeter spatial precision. To evaluate the suitability of AIIS for quantitative drug studies, caffeine was administered intravenously at doses of 1, 5, and 10 mg/kg, and the plasma concentrations were analyzed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The resulting pharmacokinetic profiles declined monoexponentially with short elimination half-lives (0.52–0.59 h) and exhibited dose-dependent changes in systemic exposure, consistent with established mouse caffeine pharmacokinetics. Overall, this study demonstrates that AIIS enables precise, reproducible, and ethically refined intravenous administration in mice and represents a practical application of physical AI for standardized in vivo preclinical research.

papers.title: PROVE: Predict-to-Specify and Observe-to-Verify for Human-Aligned Evaluation of Mobile Manipulation
papers.authors: Bowen Lyu, Yunan Liu, Liaoyuan Fan, Qinchuan Cheng, Jiafei Duan, Cheston Tan, Shijie Li
papers.abstract: Judging open-world robot manipulation is hard because layouts, articulated fixtures, and valid goal configurations vary widely. On RoboCasa365, simulator predicates agree with human judgments on only 69.09\% of rollouts, and a frontier VLM judge on 86.12\%. We present \textbf{PROVE} (Predict-to-Specify, Observe-to-Verify), which first specifies what success should look like and then checks the outcome. PROVE refines success conditions from the instruction, the initial scene, a target-object reference image, and a generated goal image. The goal image only sharpens the conditions and never serves as evidence. On 6,500 human-annotated rollouts over 65 atomic actions, PROVE reaches \textbf{96.83\%} agreement. Applied to open-source policies, it reports far lower success than native checks and changes their ranking. To reduce evaluation overhead in policy learning, we distill PROVE into \textbf{PROVE-Lite}, a 4B evaluator that needs no reference images. In one forward pass, PROVE-Lite predicts the outcome and the terminal state of each task condition. It reaches \textbf{91.20\%} agreement while running about 38$\times$ faster than PROVE. papers.title: One Patch, Many Policies: Object-Associated Physical Patch Attacks on Robotic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) are vulnerable to adversarial visual interference, motivating the study of universal and transferable physical patch attacks. Our framework combines object-associated placement, differentiable physical compositing, and final action-expert representation divergence. Physical compositing accounts for perspective and occlusion across camera views, while representation divergence guides patch optimization using either relative RMS or cosine distance. Experimental results demonstrate strong attack transferability across task suites and policies, together with the ability to selectively disrupt manipulation of an attacker-chosen task object through patch placement.

papers.title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
papers.authors: Shuaijun Liu, Qifu Wen, Xingwei Chen, Xinwen Hu, Feiyang You, Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su
papers.abstract: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. papers.title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
papers.authors: Zijia Li, Yong-Hyun Park, Shusheng Yang, Jiatao Gu
papers.abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
